title: line.split(",") turns one quoted name into two broken columns
assumption: Splitting a CSV line on "," gives you the row's fields.

input.description: An uploaded CSV where a free-text field - a person's name written "Last, First", a street address, a product description - itself contains a comma, which RFC 4180 quoting exists specifically to protect.

what_goes_wrong: `line.split(",")` on the data row produces three fields - `'"Smith'`, `' John"'`, `'100'` - instead of the two the row actually has, shifting every later naive-split column over by one.
why: A comma inside a quoted field is data, not a delimiter - RFC 4180 (and every real CSV dialect) says a field wrapped in double quotes can contain commas, newlines, or anything else, and the quotes are what tells a parser to stop treating that comma as a separator. `str.split(",")` has no concept of quoting; it is a dumb character split, so it breaks the field at the comma regardless of the surrounding quotes. A real CSV parser (Python's `csv` module) tracks quote state and only splits on commas outside quotes.

repros.code:
import csv, io
text = 'name,amount\n"Smith, John",100\n'
naive = [line.split(",") for line in text.splitlines()]
print(naive)
proper = list(csv.reader(io.StringIO(text)))
print(proper)

fix: Never parse CSV with split(","). Use a real CSV parser - Python's stdlib `csv` module, or a maintained library in JS (there is no CSV parser in the JS standard library) - that understands RFC 4180 quoting.

sources.title: RFC 4180: Common Format and MIME Type for Comma-Separated Values (CSV) Files
Python docs: csv - CSV File Reading and Writing

test_cases.note: A CSV-parsing function given this text must return two rows of two fields each, with the comma inside the quoted name preserved as part of that field's value.
